items.title: UK says EU reset deal agreed but talks will continue ‘in some areas’ – live
items.summary:
UK statement comes after EU said deal would not take effect without future agreement over university tuition fees

Senior correspondent

Making today’s reset deal contingent on a further agreement on the level of tuition fees for EU citizens is designed to neutralise the leverage London gets in the next six months, EU sources have said.

Senior diplomats had already confirmed this week that the EU would defer the deal on the level of tuition fees for another six months, a move designed to give the UK leverage in parallel negotiations to have the UK included in Made in Europe legislation designed to protect EU supply chains against China.

But the move to make the food and drink deal also contingent on a tuition fees deal effectively seeks to neutralise the leverage the UK gets today.

This is a serious chess game and shows the EU, again, is willing to speak very warmly about the UK but will play absolute hard ball when it comes to conceding any points to a former member state.

It was the same point France was making last night insisting the UK could not have voting rights on legislation in relation to food and drink.

During his meeting with businesses in Brussels, PM Burnham said his EU deal would add up to 0.5% to the UK’s GDP.

“We’re pretty much there, and it’s a really good deal.”

“Treasury analysis out today is saying that now it’s clear up to 0.5% on GDP as a result of the deal. The single…
items.t: UK says EU reset deal agreed but talks will continue ‘in some areas’ – live

items.title: JPMorgan pegs the U.S. grid fix at $1 trillion. A new study says a transformer shortage could stall it
items.summary:
A string of technology failures over the past week grounded flights, delayed bank transactions and knocked out email for millions of Americans, putting the country’s infrastructure vulnerabilities squarely in the spotlight.

The power grid has its own weak spot, and it’s made of copper and steel.

The U.S. could begin running short of the equipment that connects new power plants and data centers to the grid as early as next year, according to a new Johns Hopkins University study published in Cell Reports Sustainability . The researchers found that shortages of transformers and converters would become acute by 2030.

For businesses and households, that likely means higher electricity bills and more frequent power outages.

“This type of equipment was taken for granted but without it, you can build a data center or a power plant but it won’t be powered because you cannot connect it to the grid,” Yury Dvorkin, a Johns Hopkins associate professor who conducted the study with PhD candidate Boyu Yao, said in a university release. “When the demand for electricity started to grow faster than expected, it started to amplify all the cracks in the industry.”

Those cracks are widening fast. U.S. power use, which historically grew about 1% to 2% a year, is projected to climb 21% by 2030 as AI data centers, electric vehicles and broader electrification pile on, according to the study. Data centers alone could account for as much as two-thirds of the expected equipment shortfall. Over the longer run, the National Electrical Manufacturers Association projects U.S. electricity demand will…
items.t: JPMorgan pegs the U.S. grid fix at $1 trillion. A new study says a transformer shortage could stall it

items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
items.summary:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

items.t: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers

items.title: Anthropic’s IPO is a bellwether—and a warning
items.summary:
In today’s CEO Daily: Is the creator of Claude worth it? 

The big leadership story: A tariff refund boosts Target’s profits. 

The markets: Down globally as Anthropic’s debut fails to improve market sentiment. 

Plus: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune . 

Good morning. Anthropic just pulled off a record-breaking IPO , with the five-year-old company debuting at a value of $2 trillion. Is the creator of the Claude chatbot worth it? Will customers get enough value from its products to pay prices that justify that valuation? Is confidence in AI moving faster than companies’ ability to capitalize on it? After all, there are two ways to vote on AI: Buy the stock or buy the product. The first tells us how much capital investors are willing to commit. The second tells us whether customers get enough value to keep paying.

There are plenty of data points to discuss. Start with the org chart, which is the opposite of founder mode: CEO Dario Amodei has one direct report (Jensen Huang had 60 at Nvidia), with most of Anthropic’s senior team reporting to his sister, President Daniela Amodei. The average Anthropic employee is now worth more than $40 million . (Daniela, lunch is on you.) Anthropic’s novella-length list of risk factors about its products still reads like a dystopian sci-fi thriller . The company’s ownership structure, from the role of the Long-Term Benefit Trust to the Class F shares, can warm your heart and hurt your head. Who will decide when to speed up or slow down? 

For now, let’s look at this debut as both a bellwether of current AI sentiment and a…

items.title: Seed-oil-free foods are now a $1 billion business. Stanford scientists say the health claims don’t hold up
items.summary:
Walk down the snack aisle of almost any grocery store and you’ll find a growing number of packages labeled seed-oil-free. Americans bought more than $1 billion worth of seed-oil-free food products over the past year, according to NielsenIQ data.

Sales of seed-oil-free foods rose 60.2% over that period, while products without the label grew just 2.6%. Yet many nutrition and food scientists say those products aren’t necessarily healthier, and that seed oils aren’t harmful to people.

Seed oils are cooking oils extracted from crop seeds, including canola, corn, sunflower and safflower oil. Online influencers in the seed-oil-free movement, and the food companies serving this niche, push alternatives such as olive, avocado and coconut oil, along with animal fats like butter, lard and beef tallow, which has its own wave of celebrity backers .

Big food makers have taken notice. PepsiCo , the maker of Lay’s and Tostitos, said in 2025 that it would expand its use of avocado and olive oil in place of canola and soybean oil, one of several moves by food companies to rework products and keep up with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s vision of a healthy diet .

A seal for a growing niche 

Many seed-oil-free packages carry a Seed Oil Free Certified seal. The Seed Oil Free Alliance, a Florida-based organization founded in 2023, issues it and audits products and lab-tests their oils. The alliance says products carrying its seal account for about $410 million in retail sales, citing NielsenIQ data.

“Our organization doesn’t fearmonger about seed oils,” Jonathan Rubin, the…
items.t: Seed-oil-free foods are now a $1 billion business. Stanford scientists say the health claims don’t hold up

items.title: French AI company Mistral picks Singapore for its Asia-Pacific headquarters, bringing Europe’s ‘sovereign AI’ pitch to China’s backyard
items.summary:
Mistral is opening its Asia-Pacific headquarters in Singapore and plans to double its regional headcount to 200 by 2027, in a bet on regional interest in open-weight models. 

Chinese open-weight models—which are free for anyone to download and run on their own hardware—are already widely used in Southeast Asia. Singapore’s national AI R&D program built its latest SEA-LION model on Alibaba’s Qwen, while Singapore’s OCBC runs more than 30 internal banking tools on open models, including DeepSeek.

But Mistral thinks it can compete with Chinese providers by offering companies hands-on support. Marjorie Janiewicz, the company’s chief revenue officer, highlights three components to how to deliver an AI model: “There’s the intelligence. There’s the technology underneath to deploy it and the technology above to turn it into workflows and applications. And finally, the third component is forward-deployed engineering,” she explains.

When it comes to Chinese AI models, “usually we find that one, or multiple, of those components are missing to really get these companies to production,” she says.

Mistral’s Singapore office will also serve as an “extended Science Hub,” where the company will develop frontier models for the region’s public sector, as well as its high-tech manufacturing and robotics industries. 

“Over 70% of our team here is forward deployed engineers and scientists,” Geoff Soon, Mistral’s vice president of revenue for Asia-Pacific, says. “We’re very focused on building a deep scientific core in Singapore,” noting that almost all of their recent hires were in science…
items.t: French AI company Mistral picks Singapore for its Asia-Pacific headquarters, bringing Europe’s ‘sovereign AI’ pitch to China’s backyard

items.title: Grocers sell bananas at 66 cents a pound to lure you in. What could be the strongest El Niño on record is testing that
items.summary:
Bananas are one of the cheapest groceries at supermarkets. Americans paid just 66 cents per pound of the yellow fruit in October, compared to $2.10 for tomatoes and $2.14 for lemons, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data . But they’re about to get more expensive thanks to El Niño, which causes either wetter-or-drier-than-usual conditions for banana growers thousands of miles away. 

Less rainfall stunts bananas’ growth, which can yield harvest losses of up to 65% , and too much rainfall waterlogs the soil and incubates fungal and bacterial disease , which also reduces yields. And this year’s El Niño could be historically destructive, with about a 60% chance of the event exceeding previous El Niños dating back to 1950. 

The threat is part of why growers are asking wholesalers for more money for the fruit—and getting it—which could test bananas’ status as a loss leader for grocery stores. Costa Rica’s National Banana Corporation has recommended increasing the minimum export price of bananas by nearly 10% for next year, citing climate-driven productivity losses, a stronger currency and higher costs after seven years of no changes. Fairtrade International also approved a 5.6% increase in its average minimum prices for banana growers starting in January, citing El Niño as one of the reasons.

Francisco Martin-Rayo, CEO and cofounder of agricultural commodity price and climate risk forecaster Helios AI, told Fortune the El Niño weather extremes are “dramatically higher” and could destroy harvests next year.

“A lot of harvests will be ruined, 1,000%,” Martin-Rayo said.…
items.t: Grocers sell bananas at 66 cents a pound to lure you in. What could be the strongest El Niño on record is testing that

items.title: Disney’s sports profit jumped 53% as it bets on live games. It also wants $3 billion in cost cuts
items.summary:
Disney’s next growth era is being built around live games. ESPN will produce its first Super Bowl on Feb. 14, 2027; every Disney+ subscriber in the U.S. can stream it, and the network has just locked up exclusive rights to an expanded College Football Playoff.

For now, the bet is paying off. Disney’s Sports segment posted $4.6 billion in revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter, up 16% from a year earlier, while operating income jumped 53%. But Disney is pairing that push with a plan to cut about $3 billion in annual costs by fiscal 2029, signaling how far it is moving away from the traditional TV business that once paid for everything.

That tension defines the strategy. Disney, No. 44 on the 2026 Fortune 500 , is raising its content budget, with sports rights a major line item, while trimming the rest of the company to fund growth.

Why ESPN has become central to Disney’s strategy 

ESPN offers something most streaming libraries can’t: appointment viewing. Fans watch live, in large numbers, and advertisers pay a premium to reach them.

Disney deepened that advantage in January, when ESPN closed its acquisition of NFL Network and NFL Fantasy, along with the rights to distribute the RedZone channel to cable and satellite operators. In exchange, the NFL took a 10% stake in ESPN. Disney now holds an effective 72% interest in the network, according to its fiscal fourth-quarter shareholder letter , and Hearst owns 18%.

Audiences are rewarding the bet. Monday Night Football drew its best Week 1 and Week 2 audiences ever this season. ABC’s September broadcast of Ohio State vs.…
items.t: Disney’s sports profit jumped 53% as it bets on live games. It also wants $3 billion in cost cuts

items.title: As attention spans move on from Iran and oil, the world is forever changed and the conflict is escalating again
items.summary:
The November news cycle has fixated on elections, Nvidia , and Anthropic, but the Iran war has quietly escalated this week and there is no “credible pathway” for the world to return to its previous norm, the International Energy Agency warned in its annual World Energy Outlook released Thursday.

Even as gasoline and diesel prices have fallen from record highs in recent weeks, the Middle East will never be the same and the rest of the world is still racing to develop more of its own energy sources—both renewables and fossil fuels—as global supplies remain tight and food security is threatened in much of the world, especially Asia, the report stated. All this is transpiring as global energy demand spikes both from the AI boom and the rise of the middle class in developing countries.

“While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be. And I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said IEA executive director Fatih Birol.

The nearly nine-month Iran war and the prolonged shuttering of the vital Strait of Hormuz represent the greatest energy supply shock in modern history—far more than the Iranian Revolution or the Arab oil embargo of the 1970s—and its reverberations will be felt in ways that remain unclear, the report said. After all, the war is ongoing and Iran this week struck U.S. facilities in Bahrain and Kuwait, while the U.S. countered by striking Iran’s Qeshm Island.

“Attention is elsewhere now. I don’t know if it’s complacency…
items.t: As attention spans move on from Iran and oil, the world is forever changed and the conflict is escalating again

items.title: From losing it all to a $1 billion valuation: How Motorway’s CEO bounced back from failure
items.summary:
Tom Leathes and his two friends, Harry Jones and Alex Buttle were on a winning streak. Together, they built and sold office space platform Officila Space, broadband comparison site Top10.com, and LoanCube, a lead-generation site that was sold for $1 million. 

“We had this run of successes and thought we could do no wrong,” Leathes told Fortune. “And then we got quite schooled.” 

Their next business, a hotel recommendation app that kept the Top10 name, was their first to raise venture capital. It grew quickly, until Booking .com and the big hotel chains caught developed their own mobile apps. “All of the big hotel brands got mobile and killed us,” Leathes said. 

The founders spent two years trying to rescue the business, and a sale fell through at the last minute. They shut it down in 2015. “We lost all the money for the investors,” he said, referring to the $12.4 million the company had raised from backers including Balderton Capital and Accel. “We had to let go of the whole team.” The startup had 14 employees in London when it raised its last round in 2014. 

It was a “tough lesson,” Leathes admitted. The three went their separate ways, but within six months they were back together. “We had unfinished business,” he said. Their next venture, the trio agreed, had to be “the big one—the company that we can do for the next 10 or 20 years.” 

Leathes, Jones, and Buttle set about developing their next business idea from a disused hospital in Camden, north London, that was scheduled to be demolished. A charity had taken over the lease and was renting out the abandoned wards…

items.title: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
items.summary:
We can’t make AI safe for humanity if tech bosses are allowed to run their companies like autocracies

Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal: as the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice.

Isabelle Ferreras is accelerator fellow at the University of Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI, FNRS research director at the University of Louvain, Belgium and co-founder of DemocraticIntelligence.org
items.t: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras

items.title: ‘45 is the new 60’: Thailand’s Kasikornbank paid staff to retire early as it prepares for AI
items.summary:
Kattiya Indaravijaya sees some similarities between what’s happening in the country’s economy and what’s going on inside Kasikornbank, the company she leads as its CEO.

For the past five years, Thailand—Southeast Asia’s second-largest economy—experienced average GDP growth of just 2.34% each year , lagging behind neighboring countries like Malaysia and Vietnam that recovered more swiftly from the pandemic.

Kattiya, CEO of Kasikornbank, believes Thailand’s inability to reinvent itself is the cause of its economic rut. “We need to restructure our economy, [because] the growth engines back then are not the growth engines now,” she tells Fortune. 

Kasikornbank is now trying to find ways to boost productivity at Thailand’s third-largest bank. “Because the economy is like this, we cannot just think about revenue generation,” Kattiya explains. “[We have to consider] cost savings too, so we’re working on a lot of productivity improvements.”

A part of that was a one-time early retirement scheme, named “45 is the new 60.” Employees aged 45 to 59 could apply for voluntary early retirement, and receive both standard retirement compensation and additional severance of up to a year’s salary. 

“Those who know that technology is coming in and feel that they are unable to reskill, or feel uncomfortable, they can take this package out,” Kattiya says. “We rolled this out last year, and many people took it up… so this year our [bank’s] personnel expenses are down by quite a lot.”

items.t: ‘45 is the new 60’: Thailand’s Kasikornbank paid staff to retire early as it prepares for AI

A secretive major revamp of the Bank’s historic headquarters in the heart of London’s Square Mile presents a huge test of Bailey’s project management skills. The central bank, with its reputation staked on carefully counting the nation’s pennies, will be keen to avoid delays, budget-busting or any echoes of the expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that left his former peer Jerome Powell awkwardly clashing with Donald Trump on camera.
